title: Shloka 167
subtitle: The circle of heroes, and the point at its centre

namas.gloss: Fond Of The Company Of Heroes
namas.translation: The circle of adepts pleases her, and she is drawn to the gathering where those fit for her rites sit together.

compound.gloss: to whom the assembly of heroes is dear

children.gloss: hero, brave man; in Tantra, the adept

namas.translation: She is brave herself, and the courage she asks of her adepts is first of all her own.
Nothing ties her to what she does, so deeds pass through her without leaving the residue that binds a doer to consequences.

morphology.note: Vṛddhi derivative of niṣkarman, 'inactive'; not itself a compound.

namas.translation: She takes the form of nāda, the resonance out of which speech and world alike unfold.

morphology.note: The possessive force lies in the suffix -in, so nādarūpa is the compound and rūpiṇī the taddhita made on it; the name is also commonly read as a bahuvrīhi, she who has sound for her form.

compound.vigraha: nādasya rūpam iti nādarūpam, tad asyā astīti nādarūpiṇī

namas.translation: She sets discrimination working, rousing the faculty that tells the real from the merely apparent.

compound.gloss: the bringing forth of discriminative knowledge

children.gloss: the act of causing or bringing about

namas.translation: She is sound, unimpaired and always prepared, and the same feminine noun is used for the praise offered to her.

morphology.note: Feminine of the adjective kalya 'healthy, ready'; Monier-Williams also records a distinct f. kalyā 'praise, eulogy'.

namas.translation: She is refined and quick-witted, the participle meaning literally 'burnt through' and so ripened to perfection.

morphology.note: Past participle of vi-√dah 'burn up', which developed the transferred sense 'matured, accomplished, shrewd'.

namas.translation: Her throne is the bindu, the dimensionless point at the heart of the Śrīcakra from which every enclosure of the diagram issues.

compound.gloss: she whose seat is the central point

children.gloss: belonging to the bindu, the central point

commentary.meaning: Eight names in two lines, and the verse crosses twice from the outward setting of the rite to what stands at its centre. It opens on a gathering: the circle of vīras, the adepts qualified for the observances this school reserves for them, and she is called fond of their company before she is called anything else. The second name turns the epithet back on her — she is herself the vīrā, so that the courage asked of the circle is her own quality lent out. Then two names lift the verse off the floor of the shrine. She is beyond action, untouched by what she does; and she is nāda, the resonance from which speech and world are unfolded. The second line begins with the discernment she sets working, passes through two adjectives that describe a person rather than a principle — sound and ready, seasoned and quick — and arrives at the bindu, the dimensionless point at the centre of the Śrīcakra, which the last name gives her as a throne. Company, courage, freedom, sound, knowledge, poise, skill, seat.
commentary.history:
Vīra is ordinary Sanskrit for a man of valour, cognate with Latin vir, and it long predates any tantric use. In the Kaula literature it becomes technical. Practitioners are sorted by disposition into the paśu, the bound creature who keeps to the ordinary rules, the vīra, who is fit for observances involving what is ordinarily forbidden, and the divya, in whom the distinction has stopped mattering; and the vīra is the middle term on which most of the ritual literature concentrates, because he is the one who has something to do. Goṣṭhī began as a cow-pen, go plus a form of √sthā, then came to mean any standing-together: a company, an assembly, in classical usage a salon of cultivated talk. Vīragoṣṭhī is the seated ring of practitioners, what the texts elsewhere call the cakra, and the name says that this is where she likes to be. It is a claim about location as much as about temperament.

The second name withdraws the compliment from the assembly and gives it to her. Vīrā is the feminine of the same word, and the effect of setting it immediately after vīragoṣṭhīpriyā is to say that the quality the circle is named for does not originate in the circle. This is a move the sahasranāma makes repeatedly and never explains: an attribute is granted to her devotees and then, in the following name, claimed as hers.

Naiṣkarmyā is the strange one. The abstract noun naiṣkarmya is a vṛddhi derivative of niṣkarman, without works, and it belongs to the vocabulary of Vedānta far more than to that of tantra. The Bhagavad Gītā uses it in its third chapter to make a point that is nearly the opposite of what the word suggests: freedom from action is not reached by declining to act. Śaṅkara's pupil Sureśvara wrote a whole treatise called the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi on what the state amounts to. Its appearance here, two names after the circle of adepts, in a hymn whose entire apparatus is ritual activity, is worth pausing over. The commentators generally take it to mean that her acts of creating, maintaining and withdrawing the world leave no residue on her, being play rather than obligation; the practical corollary, which the rest of the verse will develop, is that nothing done in front of her diagram is a transaction either.

Nāda comes from √nad, to sound or roar, but in this literature it does not mean audible noise. It names the first stirring of sound before articulation, the middle term in the sequence bindu, nāda, kalā by which the schools of mantra describe the unfolding of the absolute into speech, and it corresponds to the levels of the word — parā, paśyantī, madhyamā, vaikharī — of which only the last reaches the ear. To call her nādarūpiṇī immediately after calling her actionless is to block a misreading: what is beyond action is not thereby inert. It resounds, and everything audible is downstream of it.

The second line changes register. Vijñānakalanā is built on √kal, to impel or bring about, so the sense is that she is the setting-in-motion of discriminative knowledge rather than the knowledge itself. Kalyā carries two lexical lives at once: as the feminine of the adjective kalya it means whole, sound, in good health, ready — the same stem gives kalya for daybreak, the hour when one is fit for work — while Monier-Williams also records a separate feminine noun kalyā meaning praise. A hymn is not obliged to choose. Vidagdhā is the past participle of vi-√dah, burnt up, and its transferred sense is one of the most characteristic words of courtly Sanskrit: the vidagdha is the connoisseur, the person of finished taste, on the metaphor of clay fired hard or gold burnt clean. That this vocabulary of the literary salon should appear in a tantric hymn is not an accident; the goṣṭhī of the first name is the same social form that the poets used.

Baindava is the vṛddhi adjective from bindu, a drop, a dot, the point without magnitude. As a seat it means the centre of the Śrīcakra, where the diagram's nine enclosures converge and where the goddess is invoked before any offering is made. The verse thus ends exactly where the diagram ends, and the reader who has followed the eight names from the outer ring of adepts to the innermost point has traced the same path inward that the ritual takes.
commentary.practice:
The metre is anuṣṭubh and the syllable count falls out cleanly: six syllables of vīragoṣṭhīpriyā plus two of vīrā make the first eight, three of naiṣkarmyā plus five of nādarūpiṇī make the second. The caesura is at the end of nādarūpiṇī, sixteen syllables in, and that is the only place to breathe.

Three clusters in this verse cause most of the trouble. In goṣṭhī the ṣṭh is a retroflex sibilant followed by an aspirated retroflex stop: the tongue curls back for ṣ and stays back for ṭh, and the h is breath released through the same closure, not a separate syllable. In naiṣkarmyā the sequence rmy runs a retroflex-tinged r into a labial m into a palatal y with no vowel between them; English speakers insert one almost involuntarily, producing something like narish-karamya. Say kar, then close the lips for m, then release directly into yā. And in vidagdhā the g and dh are both voiced, the second aspirated — g, then d with breath, then ā — which is easier if you slow the word to three deliberate beats before restoring speed.

The jñ of vijñānakalanā is pronounced differently across India. The southern recitation traditions that carry this stotra generally give it as a palatal j followed by the palatal nasal ñ; much of the north says gya. Either will be understood; consistency within a recitation matters more than the choice.

Baindavāsanā hides a join. The elements are baindava and āsana, and the final short a of the first meets the long ā of the second to give a single long ā: baindav-āsanā. The opening ai is a full diphthong of two morae, not the clipped English vowel of "bite". The same diphthong appeared in mahāsanā's cousin earlier in the hymn, and the two names should be heard together — she is seated on the great seat, and the great seat is a point.

For recitation as archanā the names take the dative. The ā-stems give vīragoṣṭhīpriyāyai, vīrāyai, naiṣkarmyāyai, vijñānakalanāyai, kalyāyai, vidagdhāyai, baindavāsanāyai, all in -āyai; nādarūpiṇī, being an ī-stem, gives nādarūpiṇyai. The verse is a good place to hear the difference between the two endings, since seven of the eight take one and one takes the other.

What the verse asks is set by its second name and its third. Most people who chant this stotra do so alone, and the first name describes a circle; the tradition's own answer is that the recitation joins one to a company that is not assembled in the room. The third name is the harder demand. Naiṣkarmyā stands two syllables from the beginning of a hymn that will later promise results, and it says of her that action leaves no mark. Chanted honestly it asks the reciter to stop keeping accounts of the recitation.

crossReferences.deva: न कर्मणामनारम्भान्नैष्कर्म्यं पुरुषोऽश्नुते । न च संन्यसनादेव सिद्धिं समधिगच्छति ॥
crossReferences.iast: na karmaṇām anārambhān naiṣkarmyaṃ puruṣo 'śnute | na ca saṃnyasanād eva siddhiṃ samadhigacchati ||
crossReferences.translation: A man does not attain freedom from action by not undertaking actions, nor does he reach perfection by renunciation alone.
crossReferences.relevance: The locus classicus for naiṣkarmya, and the reason the name in this verse cannot mean idleness. The Gītā's point is that actionlessness is a condition of the agent, not a description of his schedule, which is exactly what is needed to make sense of an epithet applied to a goddess who is elsewhere in this hymn said to create, sustain and withdraw the worlds.

crossReferences.deva: ओमित्येतदक्षरमिदं सर्वं तस्योपव्याख्यानं भूतं भवद्भविष्यदिति सर्वमोङ्कार एव । यच्चान्यत्त्रिकालातीतं तदप्योङ्कार एव ॥
crossReferences.iast: om ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvaṃ tasyopavyākhyānaṃ bhūtaṃ bhavad bhaviṣyad iti sarvam oṃkāra eva | yac cānyat trikālātītaṃ tad apy oṃkāra eva ||
crossReferences.translation: Oṃ — this syllable is all this. Its explanation follows. What was, what is, what will be: all of it is simply oṃ. And whatever else there is beyond the three times, that too is simply oṃ.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest compact statement of the position that nādarūpiṇī assumes: that sound is not something the world contains but something the world consists of. The Upaniṣad's later analysis of oṃ into its constituent measures, and of a fourth beyond them, is the source from which the tantric schema of bindu, nāda and kalā is developed.

references.title: Lalitā Sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Theosophical Publishing House / Adyar)
references.note: The only complete English rendering of the commentary that the tradition itself treats as authoritative. It is a nineteenth-century translation and reads like one, but for a verse like this it is indispensable, because it shows how a learned eighteenth-century reader handled a name such as naiṣkarmyā that comes from outside the tantric lexicon.

references.title: The Secret of the Three Cities: An Introduction to Hindu Śākta Tantrism
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (University of Chicago Press, 1990)
references.note: The best first book on Śrīvidyā in English, and the place to go for what vīra means as a category rather than as a compliment. Brooks is careful about the difference between what the texts prescribe and what practitioners in South India actually do, which matters for a name like vīragoṣṭhīpriyā.

references.title: Sonic Theology: Hinduism and Sacred Sound
references.author: Guy L. Beck (University of South Carolina Press, 1993)
references.note: A survey of the Indian doctrines of sound from the Vedic period onward, and the most accessible account of nāda for someone who has met the word only in a hymn. Read it if nādarūpiṇī sounds like poetry to you; it is a technical claim with a long argumentative history behind it.

references.title: Kulārṇava Tantra
references.author: ed. Tārānātha Vidyāratna, with an introduction by Arthur Avalon
references.note: The classic Kaula handbook, and the text in which the vocabulary of the vīra and of the assembled circle is laid out at length rather than alluded to. Its tone is unlike the sahasranāma's — blunt, hortatory, much concerned with who is and is not qualified — and the contrast is instructive.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Worth opening at kalyā and at vidagdha specifically. The first entry shows two distinct feminine nouns sitting on the same form, one meaning health and readiness and one meaning praise; the second shows how a participle meaning burnt came to mean sophisticated. Both are cases where the dictionary explains a name better than any commentary does.
